Noted — and the combination is coherent: it verifies, executes what works on your go, and when something's broken it says so and stops rather than trying to fix or escalate.

Four more.

questions.question: The spec covers deploys, release cuts, tagging and releases — plus env-var sync, MRT state and rollback. Those are distinct operations with different risk. How should the skill be entered?

options.label: Named modes
options.description: `status` (default) · `deploy <env> <ref>` · `tag <version>` · `release` (the full cut) · `sync-env <env>` · `rollback <env>`. You say what you want; the skill verifies the gates for that operation only. Fastest, and each mode can carry its own preflight.

options.label: One flow that asks
options.description: Invoke it bare, it reports state and asks what you want to do via AskUserQuestion. Fewer things to remember, and you always see the state before choosing — but every routine env-var sync starts with a full status pass.

options.label: Status by default, everything else explicit
options.description: Bare invocation always reports state and stops. Any action needs an explicit mode argument, so nothing can ever run by accident from a bare call.

questions.question: You've said everything executes on your explicit go. But an RC tag is permanently undeletable by anyone, and a prod deploy has nothing between it and production. Should the confirmation for those look different from, say, an env-var sync to dev?

options.label: Show the exact command and its consequence, then confirm
options.description: For anything irreversible the skill prints the literal command it will run, states plainly what cannot be undone — 'this tag cannot be deleted by anyone, including you' — and waits. Same gate mechanism as elsewhere, but you see exactly what lands.

options.label: Require you to type the tag or environment name back
options.description: A second, deliberate confirmation for irreversible actions specifically — you retype `v0.1.0-rc.3` or `prod`. Harder to fire by reflex when you're moving fast, at the cost of friction on every one.

options.label: Same confirmation as everything else
options.description: One consistent gate for all actions. Simplest to reason about; treats a permanent tag and a dev env-var sync identically.

questions.question: tagging.md documents two rollback paths: emergency (re-activate a previous MRT bundle by hand, then record it) and controlled (`deploy-*.yml -f rollback=true`, which skips the version downgrade guard). Its only stated human gate is environment required reviewers — which we verified do not exist on any environment.

options.label: Support it, and say plainly that it's ungated
options.description: The skill can run a rollback on your go, but states before it does that `rollback=true` bypasses the downgrade guard and that no environment reviewer exists to catch a mistake. You proceed knowing exactly what is and isn't protecting you.

options.label: Prepare it, never run it
options.description: Rollback is the one thing the skill only ever hands you as a command. It's the action most likely to be taken under pressure, on the worst day, and it's the one with no safety net at all.

options.label: Leave rollback out entirely
options.description: Out of scope for now. Revisit once environment protection rules exist and the path has a real gate.

questions.question: The repo has two skills that belong in a release flow: /generate-changelog (tagging.md says run it before cutting a release branch) and /upstream-sync-review (before bumping the Salesforce base). Both already exist and are the team's.

options.label: Call both at the right points
options.description: The release flow invokes /generate-changelog before a cut, and DevOps offers /upstream-sync-review when the upstream watcher flags a new version. Reuses the team's tooling rather than duplicating it — consistent with how PreBuild calls /feature-spec and /scope-check.

options.label: Call /generate-changelog only
options.description: Changelog generation is genuinely part of cutting a release. Upstream bumps are a separate piece of work with their own cadence, and pulling them into DevOps blurs the boundary.

options.label: Neither — point at them instead
options.description: The skill names them at the right moment and you invoke them. Keeps DevOps focused on state and execution, and keeps each skill's output something you saw directly.

content.text:
All ruled. Here's the proposal.

## `zimmerMANNDevOps` — proposed shape

**Posture:** verify live, then execute what's actually possible. `DEVOPS-STATE.md` is a list of things to re-check, never a source of fact — everything in it was documented-as-working while broken, and it will go stale the same way.

### Modes

| Mode | Does |
|---|---|
| `status` *(default, and a bare call stops here)* | Full live state: gate health, environment rules, tag state, workflow run history, what is currently possible |
| `deploy <env> <ref>` | Preflight that environment, then dispatch on your go |
| `tag <version>` | Validate the name against both rulesets and the hook, check `tag-validate.yml` is even present on this branch, then cut on your go |
| `release` | The full cut — calls `/generate-changelog` first, per `tagging.md` |
| `sync-env <env>` | `sync-env-vars-to-mrt.yml`, with prod excluded by design |
| `rollback <env>` | Both documented paths, with the gap stated up front |

### Preflight — re-derived every run, never cached

For whichever mode you're in: environment protection rules · whether `SIT Gate` can pass (does a `*.p0.spec` exist, are the `LHCI_*` secrets present, is `RETAIL_APP_HOME` set) · does `prod` have env vars in GitHub · is `tag-validate.yml` on the branch being tagged · do the undeclared binaries still resolve · recent run history for the workflow about to fire.

### Irreversible actions

Print the literal command, state the consequence in plain terms, then wait. For a tag that means saying outright: **"this tag cannot be deleted or moved by anyone, including you — the `tag-rc` ruleset has zero bypass actors."** For a prod deploy: **"no environment reviewer exists; `versionGuard` skips any ref that isn't a `v*` tag."**

### Broken gates

Report with evidence, name the owner, **stop.** No fixing, no drafting the escalation. `.github/workflows/` and environment config are Tier 1 and not yours.

### Rollback

Supported on your go, and it says before running that `rollback=true` bypasses the downgrade guard and that no environment reviewer exists to catch a mistake.

### The naming table goes in the skill

`prod` (GitHub Environment, `versionGuard`, `.env.prod`) · `production` (config file, `DEPLOY_TARGET`, **the MRT target**) · `master` (Contentful). It has to be in there because `README.md:78` is wrong on the one tier with no automated sync.

## Agents

**None.** This is state verification and execution, not a loop — no implement/test/score cycle to run. `zm-tester` and the rest have nothing to do here. Say if you'd rather it fanned out for the status pass.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `skills/zimmerMANNDevOps/SKILL.md` | **new** |
| everything else | untouched |

One thing I'd flag: `status` will be slow — it's a dozen live API calls before it says anything. That's the cost of the choice you made, and I think it's the right one, but you'll feel it on routine invocations.

Go ahead?

content.text:
All twelve decisions in. Final proposal.

## `zimmerMANNDevOps`

**Primary use is deploys and promotions**, with release cuts as the occasional path.

### Modes

`status` *(default; bare call stops here)* · `deploy <env> <ref>` · `promote <from> <to>` · `tag <version>` · `release` · `sync-env <env>` · `rollback <env>`

`deploy-dev` and `deploy-sit` are **not dispatchable** — dev fires on push to `develop`, sit only on a successful SIT Gate. The skill says so rather than pretending otherwise.

### Every invocation

**Full pipeline health preflight** — SIT Gate viability, environment rules, tag state, workflow history, undeclared binaries — then **the full ladder**: what ref each of the six environments is running and how stale it is. You see the whole picture before moving one rung.

### The ref rule

**Tags for uat, staging and prod. Branch refs allowed on test** for on-demand looks. The skill refuses a branch ref above test unless you explicitly override, and says why: `versionGuard` skips anything that isn't a `v*` tag, so a branch ref means nothing is stopping a downgrade.

Worth being upfront — **this will bite the first time you promote to uat**, because every deploy to date has been `ref=develop`. That's the point of choosing it, but it'll feel obstructive on day one.

### Promotion order

`uat → staging → prod`, per `tagging.md` as the Tier 1 source. Where a promotion also touches Contentful, the skill notes that **content promotes staging-before-uat** and leaves that call to you.

### Irreversible actions

Print the literal command, state the consequence plainly, wait. For a tag: *"this cannot be deleted or moved by anyone, including you."* For prod: *"no environment reviewer exists; versionGuard will skip this ref."*

### Rollback

Supported on your go, prefaced with the gap: `rollback=true` bypasses the downgrade guard and nothing else is watching.

### Broken gates

Report with evidence, name the owner, **stop.** Tier 1 config isn't yours to fix.

### Reuse

`/generate-changelog` before a release cut · `/upstream-sync-review` when the upstream watcher flags a version.

### The naming table, in the skill

`prod` = GitHub Environment, `versionGuard`, `.env.prod` · `production` = config file, `DEPLOY_TARGET`, **the MRT target** · `master` = Contentful. `README.md:78` gets this wrong on the one tier with no automated sync.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `skills/zimmerMANNDevOps/SKILL.md` | **new** |
| everything else | untouched. **No agents** — this is verification and execution, not a loop. |

One honest note: you've chosen thoroughness at every fork, so `deploy test develop` will run a dozen API calls before it dispatches. That's the right trade for something that touches environments, but you'll feel it.

Go ahead?

set -e
S=~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/skills/zimmerMANNDevOps
mkdir -p "$S"
cat > "$S/SKILL.md" <<'SKILLEOF'
---
name: zimmerMANNDevOps
description: Runs deploys, promotions across environments, tags, release cuts and rollbacks on the Zimmermann PWA Kit. Verifies pipeline state live before every action, shows what each environment is running, and executes only on explicit approval. Reports broken gates and stops rather than working around them.
---

Deploys and promotions are the everyday use. Release cuts are the occasional one.

**Verify before you advise.** Every claim about this pipeline that was written down has been wrong
somewhere — `tagging.md` describes sprint tagging that is dead, `README.md:78` names the wrong MRT
target, Confluence carries three different promotion orders. `.research/DEVOPS-STATE.md` is a list
of things to re-check, **never a source of fact.** Derive state live, every time.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

---

## Modes

| Mode | Does |
|---|---|
| `status` *(default)* | Full state. A bare invocation stops here. |
| `deploy <env> <ref>` | Preflight, then dispatch on approval |
| `promote <from> <to>` | Takes what `<from>` is running and deploys it to `<to>` |
| `tag <version>` | Validates the name, checks the tag workflow is even present, cuts on approval |
| `release` | The full cut — changelog, tag, promote |
| `sync-env <env>` | `sync-env-vars-to-mrt.yml`. Prod is excluded by design. |
| `rollback <env>` | Either documented path, with the gap stated first |

**Two workflows are not dispatchable.** `deploy-dev.yml` fires only on push to `develop`.
`deploy-sit.yml` fires only on a successful `SIT Gate` `workflow_run`. If asked to deploy either,
say so and explain what actually triggers them — do not attempt a dispatch that will fail.

---

## Every invocation starts here

### 1. The ladder — what is each environment running?

```bash
for e in dev test sit uat staging prod; do
  gh api "repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/deployments?environment=$e&per_page=1" \
    --jq 'if length==0 then "never deployed" else "\(.[0].ref) @ \(.[0].sha[:7]) — \(.[0].created_at[:10])" end'
done
```

Print all six with their age. **Flag staleness** — an environment weeks behind the one below it is
the context you would otherwise reconstruct by hand, and it changes whether a promotion is routine
or a leap.

### 2. Pipeline health

- **Environment protection rules** — `gh api repos/.../environments/<env>`. Report `protection_rules`
  and `deployment_branch_policy` honestly. As of the last check every environment returned `[]` and
  `null`, meaning no reviewer stands between a dispatch and that environment.
- **Can `SIT Gate` pass?** Does any `**/*.p0.spec.{js,ts}` exist · are `LHCI_SERVER_BASE_URL`,
  `LHCI_TOKEN`, `LHCI_TARGET_URL_SIT` present · is `RETAIL_APP_HOME` set anywhere the job can read.
  If not, `release/**` merges are blocked and `deploy-sit.yml` cannot fire.
- **Does the target environment have the vars this deploy needs?** `prod` has historically held
  none — its MRT vars are set by hand in the console.
- **Recent runs of the workflow about to fire** — `gh api .../workflows/<file>/runs`. A workflow
  with zero runs is about to execute for the first time. Say so.
- **Do the undeclared binaries still resolve?** `bundlesize`, `cross-env` and `@lhci/cli` are not in
  `package.json`; they arrive transitively through `@salesforce/retail-react-app`.

---

## Which ref may go where

| Tier | Accepts |
|---|---|
| `dev` | not dispatchable — auto on push to `develop` |
| `test` | a tag **or** a branch ref, for on-demand looks |
| `sit` | not dispatchable — `workflow_run` off `SIT Gate` |
| `uat`, `staging`, `prod` | **a `vX.Y.Z` tag** |

**Refuse a branch ref above `test`** unless explicitly overridden, and give the reason:
`versionGuard.mjs` skips any ref that is not a `v*` tag, so a branch ref means the downgrade guard
does not run — nothing prevents deploying something older than what is live.

Expect this to bite. **Every deployment to date has used `ref=develop`**, so the first tag-based
promotion will be the first time this rule has ever applied.

## Promotion order

`uat → staging → prod`, per `.claude/rules/tagging.md` as the Tier 1 source.

**Where a promotion also involves Contentful, say so:** `contentfulMapping.ts` and the Contentful
scripts promote content **staging before uat** — the opposite order. Both are internally consistent
and nothing explains the difference. Surface it and let Marcel decide; do not silently pick.

## The three namespaces

| Name | Where it is the truth |
|---|---|
| `prod` | GitHub Environment · `versionGuard` argument · `.env.prod` · `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` |
| `production` | `config/production.js` · `DEPLOY_TARGET` · **the MRT target** (`push:prod` → `-t production`) |
| `master` | the Contentful environment |

`README.md:78` tells a tier-1 approver to set production env vars in the MRT console under `prod`.
**The target is `production`.** Production is the one tier with no automated var sync, so this is
the only path — use the right name.

---

## Executing

Nothing runs without approval. Present, then wait.

For **irreversible** actions, print the literal command and state the consequence plainly before
asking:

- **Any tag** — *"This tag cannot be deleted or moved by anyone, including you. The `tag-rc` ruleset
  has zero bypass actors."*
- **A deploy to `prod`** — *"No environment reviewer exists. `versionGuard` will "* + (skip this ref
  / block a downgrade), whichever is true for the ref in hand.
- **Any first-ever run of a workflow** — *"`deploy-stg.yml` has never executed. This is its first run."*

Then dispatch:

```bash
gh workflow run deploy-<env>.yml -f ref=<ref>
```

Report the run URL, watch it to completion, and report the real outcome — not the dispatch's exit code.

## Tagging

Before cutting any tag:

1. **Validate the name** against both patterns — `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+-rc\.\d+$` and
   `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-hotfix\.\d+)?$`. Nothing else is accepted anywhere, and **no layer matches
   anything but lowercase `v*`** — `V0.1.0` or `0.1.0` slips past the hook, the workflow and both
   rulesets.
2. **Check `tag-validate.yml` exists on the branch being tagged.** GitHub evaluates a tag workflow
   from the tagged commit; the file has historically lived only on `develop`, so a tag cut from a
   release branch is not validated at all. Say which is true right now.
3. **Annotated only** — `git tag -a <tag> -m "<message>"`. Never lightweight. Never `npm version`;
   its commit is blocked by `release/**` protection.
4. **Push the tag alone** — `git push origin <tag>`.

## Rollback

Both paths, and state the gap before either:

> `rollback=true` skips the version downgrade guard, and no environment required reviewer exists to
> catch a mistake. Nothing else is watching this.

- **Controlled** — `gh workflow run deploy-<env>.yml -f ref=<previous-tag> -f rollback=true`
- **Emergency** — re-activate the previous MRT bundle by hand, then
  `node scripts/versionGuard.mjs record <env> <ref>` so the Deployment record matches reality

## Release cut

1. `/generate-changelog` — the team's skill, and `tagging.md` says run it before cutting
2. Cut `release/vX.Y.Z` from `develop`
3. RC tags as needed, each deployed to `test`
4. Merge to `main`, bump `package.json` (Tier 1 — needs an approver)
5. Final `vX.Y.Z` tag on the merge commit — tier-1-approvers only
6. Promote `uat → staging → prod`
7. Back-merge to `develop` — required by `.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md`, enforced by nothing

Offer `/upstream-sync-review` when the upstream watcher has flagged a new base version.

---

## When a gate is broken

**Report it, name the owner, and stop.**

Do not work around it, do not fix it, do not draft the escalation. `.github/workflows/` and
environment configuration are **Tier 1**, owned by Integration / SI Partner, routed to
`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` by `CODEOWNERS`. Not yours to change.

Give the evidence — the command, its real output, the file and line — so the report stands on its
own when Marcel takes it to whoever owns it.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never dispatch, tag, push or roll back without explicit approval.**
- **Never modify `.github/workflows/`, `config/`, `package.json`, `.claude/**` or any Tier 1 file.**
- **Never present cached state as current.** If you did not check it this run, say so.
- **Never claim a deploy succeeded from the dispatch's exit code.** Watch the run.
- **Never guess an MRT target name.** `production`, not `prod`.
- **Say what you could not verify** — MRT console state is not reachable from here, and that
  includes what production's env vars actually are.

All eight decisions in. Here's the proposal.

## `zimmerMANNSprinter`

**Sources:** Jira and Confluence. **Trello is explicitly out of scope** — no connector exists and none is in the registry. The skill says so rather than implying coverage.

### Modes

**`refine <keys>`** — the method your transcripts already show, encoded:

Per story, the 7-point sizing lens — FE impact? · clear enough to size? · which surfaces (PWA Kit/React, Contentful, SFCC integration, checkout, account, PDP/PLP, CMS)? · design/Figma dependencies? · API/backend dependencies? · pure FE, shared, or needs architecture? · size now or clarify first? — then the four standing axes: **behaviour · desktop/mobile · a11y · data.**

Plus **design-dependency flagging**: any story blocked on design componentization gets called out explicitly. That's the one that silently sinks a commitment.

Output is a question list you can take into the room, not a verdict.

**`plan <sprint>`** — per candidate: refined? has ACs? design signed off? what does it depend on? what's blocking it. Then a **sequencing suggestion** — design-dependent work last, shared-component work first. Capacity and assignment stay out; the skill has no basis to model who's on leave.

**`standup`** — derives your commits, PR activity and Jira transitions since the last standup and drafts the factual half. Then **asks what's blocking you** rather than guessing.

**`retro <sprint>`** — Jira and git for the sprint (committed versus shipped, carried over, reopened, time sitting in review) plus any `.runs/<TICKET>/` artefacts. Factual input to a human conversation, not an opinion about it.

**`prep <invite>`** — paste any meeting invite. Reads the agenda, attendees and stated objectives and shapes prep around that specific meeting. Covers the ceremonies and the alignment calls, TNL sessions and vendor meetings your transcripts are full of.

### Writes

On your explicit go — estimates, comments, transitions. Shown exactly before they land.

**And the phrasing rule applies**, since a Jira comment is outward-facing: where the owner is senior or lateral, phrased as a question, never a directive.

### Two things carried from the transcripts

*"No overthinking, straightforward, work with what we have and not with what we lack."* And the BA/dev split you ratified: **BAs work at component level, devs take the atomic level** — refinement questions should sit at the right altitude for who's in the room.

## Agents

**My recommendation, not a decision:** fan out for multi-ticket refinement only — one general-purpose agent per ticket when you pass several keys, since that's a genuinely parallel read. Sequential otherwise. **Not** the `zm-*` set; those are build-loop roles and don't fit here.

Say if you'd rather it stayed sequential throughout.

| everything else | untouched |

set -e
S=~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/skills/zimmerMANNSprinter
mkdir -p "$S"
cat > "$S/SKILL.md" <<'SKILLEOF'
---
name: zimmerMANNSprinter
description: The skill for sprint and agile ceremonies as FED Lead — backlog refinement, sprint planning, standups, retros, and prep for any meeting. Reads Jira and Confluence, drafts what you need to take into the room, and writes to Jira only on your explicit go.
---

For the ceremonies. Reads the board and the docs, gives you what you need to walk into the room
with, and never speaks on your behalf without you seeing it first.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**Sources: Jira and Confluence.** Trello is named in the original spec but **there is no MCP
connector for it and none in the registry** — it is outside what this skill can see. Say so rather
than implying coverage.

**No overthinking. Straightforward. Work with what we have, not with what we lack.** Run a sanity
check on anything before it goes to a colleague — a question raised at the wrong altitude costs
more than one not raised.

---

## Modes

`refine <keys>` · `plan <sprint>` · `standup` · `retro <sprint>` · `prep <invite>`

Any mode accepts a pasted meeting invite as extra context.

---

## `refine <keys>` — backlog refinement

For each story, run the sizing lens and the four axes. Output is **a question list you can take
into the room**, not a verdict.

### The seven-point sizing lens

1. Is there any **front-end impact**?
2. Is the requirement **clear enough to size**?
3. **Which surfaces** does it touch — PWA Kit / React, Contentful, SFCC integration, checkout,
   account, PDP/PLP, CMS-rendered?
4. Are there **design / Figma dependencies**?
5. Are there **API / backend dependencies**?
6. Is this **pure FE**, a shared FE/BE change, or does it need **architecture input**?
7. Can we **size now**, or do we need clarification first?

### The four standing axes

Every story gets read for: **behaviour · desktop/mobile · a11y · data.**

Those four are where the ambiguity usually hides, and they are the questions worth asking while
the BA and the designer are still in the room.

### Design dependency — call it out explicitly

A story blocked on design componentization **cannot be picked up**, however well it is written.
Check the linked Figma: does the design exist, is it current rather than archived, are all variants
and states drawn. Flag every story where the answer is no, by name.

This is the one that silently sinks a sprint commitment. It has happened before.

### Altitude

**BAs work at the component level; devs take the atomic level.** Pitch each question for whoever
owns the answer. A question about atom decomposition is not a refinement question — it is a
build decision, and raising it here wastes the room's time.

### Output

Per story: the seven answers, the four axes with anything unclear flagged, design status, and
**the specific questions to raise, with who should answer each.** Then a one-line readiness call —
sizeable now, or blocked on X.

---

## `plan <sprint>` — sprint planning

For each candidate story:

- **Refined?** Has it been through refinement, and did anything come out unresolved?
- **Has acceptance criteria?** Actual ACs, not a description.
- **Design signed off?** Not "design exists" — signed off.
- **What does it depend on?** Other stories, another squad, an integration, a decision.
- **What is blocking it right now?**

Then a **sequencing suggestion**: design-dependent work last, shared-component work first, and
anything that unblocks another story ahead of the thing it unblocks. State the reasoning so it can
be argued with.

**Capacity and assignment stay out.** The skill does not know who is on leave, who is carrying
support, or how the team feels about the load. That is the room's conversation.

---

## `standup`

Derive the factual half. Ask for the rest.

**What you did** — commits authored since the last standup, PRs opened, reviewed or merged, Jira
transitions on your tickets.

```bash
git log --author="$(git config user.email)" --since="yesterday" --oneline
gh pr list --author "@me" --state all --limit 10 --json number,title,state,updatedAt
```

Plus Jira transitions on tickets assigned to you.

**What you are doing** — from the tickets in progress and the branch you are on.

**What is blocking you** — **ask.** Do not infer it. A PR sitting unreviewed for two days might be
a blocker or might be fine, and only you know which.

Keep it short. This is a two-minute update, not a report.

---

## `retro <sprint>`

Factual input to a human conversation. Not an opinion about how the sprint went.

- **Committed versus shipped** — what went into the sprint, what closed.
- **Carried over** — and how many sprints each has now carried.
- **Reopened** — anything that went back to In Progress after being called done.
- **Time in review** — how long PRs sat before first review and before merge.
- **Build run artefacts** — anything under `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/`: rework rounds
  per step, what the Scorer kept returning, what a loop could not verify.

Present the numbers and stop. **Do not editorialise.** The team decides what any of it means, and
a retro pre-loaded with conclusions steers toward what is measurable rather than what mattered.

---

## `prep <invite>`

Paste any meeting invite — ceremony or not. Alignment calls, TNL sessions, vendor sessions,
design reviews.

Read the **agenda, the attendees and the stated objectives**, then prepare for that specific
meeting rather than a generic template:

- What is this meeting actually for, in one line
- What each attendee will want from you
- What you need to know before walking in — from Jira, Confluence, the codebase
- **The questions worth asking**, and who to ask each
- Anything you should have an answer ready for
- Anything genuinely outside your remit, named as such

---

## Writing to Jira

Estimates, comments, transitions and AC edits all go on a shared board under your name.

**Draft it, show it, write it on your explicit go.** Never before.

And because it is outward-facing, the phrasing rule applies: **where the owner is senior or
lateral, phrase it as a question, never a directive.** Ask confirmatorily. Before anything posts,
count the asks — a comment that tags one person five times reads as hiding behind their authority.

---

## Output

**"ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead"** register — not dumbed down, but without jargon that gets in the
way. Lead with the consequence.

Put decisions to Marcel **one at a time, using AskUserQuestion.** Never a wall of choices.

Where the output is a message to a person — Teams, a Jira comment, an email — write it in **natural
human language without sacrificing the technical accuracy.** No em-dashes. No AI tells. It should
read as though he wrote it, because he is the one sending it.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never write to Jira or Confluence without an explicit go.**
- **Never invent an acceptance criterion, an estimate, or a dependency.** If it is not in the
  ticket, it is a question, not a finding.
- **Never claim Trello coverage.** It is not connected.
- **Never model capacity or assign work.** Not the skill's call.
- **Never editorialise a retro.**
- **Say what you could not check.** A ticket you could not read, a Confluence page that 404s, a
  design link that is dead — each is itself worth raising.

**Skill #6 built** — 189 lines. Repo untouched. Six of eight.

Five modes: `refine` · `plan` · `standup` · `retro` · `prep`, any of which takes a pasted invite as context.

**`refine` carries your actual method** — the seven-point sizing lens, the four standing axes, and explicit design-dependency flagging. It fans out one agent per ticket when you pass several keys and stays sequential for one. Output is a question list with who should answer each, not a verdict.

content.text:
All seven decisions in. Here's the proposal.

## `zimmerMANNDevImprover`

**Invocation:** `devimprove <TICKET> [<TICKET>…]` — you name the stories.

### What it reads

Session transcripts for those keys from `~/.claude/projects/…zimmermann-pwa/` plus their `subagents/` transcripts · `.runs/<TICKET>/plan.md` and `findings.md` where they exist · the current skill and agent files · and the repo itself, to re-resolve what the skills cite.

### Two jobs

**Job A — how the loop performed.** For each failure, whose gap it was:

*Plan gap* (step underspecified, criteria unmeasurable) · *Implementer gap* · *Tester gap* (a defect reached the Scorer) · *Scorer gap* (passed something it shouldn't, or returned without a usable instruction) · **Brief gap** — the instruction itself was wrong, which was the most common class in your historical runs · *Rule gap* — the codebase rule is wrong, missing, or contradicts another.

Any genuine defect qualifies. **Recurrence isn't the bar, but it is the strongest signal** and gets called out as such.

**Job B — citation drift.** Every `file:line` and rule the skills cite, re-resolved against the current repo. The `var(--zimm-*)` boundary reversed twice in a fortnight; `tagging.md` still describes sprint tagging that's dead. This is the failure mode that made the FED handbook stale, and it's cheap to check.

### What it may change

The three build skills — **PreBuild, Build, PostBuild** — and the **five loop agents**, since that's where the behaviour actually lives.

**Out of bounds: Review, Sprinter, DevOps, and itself.** Review belongs to RevImprover. It never edits its own judgement criteria.

### Output

Per proposal: the file · the current text · the replacement · the evidence, cited to a transcript turn or a `file:line`. **Paste-ready. "Be more careful" is not a proposal.**

Presented one at a time via AskUserQuestion. **Applies on your explicit go.**

### One addition I'd make

**It writes its own findings log** to `.runs/_improver/<date>.md` — including things it saw but didn't propose. Without that, "recurrence is the strongest signal" can't work: nothing else remembers what a previous run observed, and we dropped the tracker that would have. Recording is free; it's the memory the skill needs to spot a second occurrence.

Say if you'd rather it kept no record.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `skills/zimmerMANNDevImprover/SKILL.md` | **new** |
| everything else | untouched — it proposes edits, it doesn't ship with any |

Go ahead?

Reads the session transcripts and run artefacts for named stories, diagnoses where the loop failed and whose gap it was, checks whether the skills still cite things that are true, and proposes concrete edits to the build skills and loop agents — applied only on Marcel's explicit go.

The look-back. It reads how build work actually went, works out what would have prevented each
failure, and proposes the specific edit that does it.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**Input:** `$ARGUMENTS` — one or more Jira keys. `devimprove SFCC-89 SFCC-194`.

There is no in-loop observer feeding this skill — `zm-tracker` was deliberately dropped, so
improvement is post-hoc and reconstructed. Everything below is evidence you have to go and find.

---

## What you read

**1. The session transcripts.** For each key, find the sessions that mention it:

```bash
D=~/.claude/projects/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev-zimmermann-pwa
grep -l "SFCC-89" "$D"/*.jsonl
```

Read those sessions and their `<session-uuid>/subagents/*.jsonl` transcripts. The `.meta.json`
sidecar next to each gives `agentType` and `description`, so you can tell which loop role a
transcript belongs to without reading it.

This is unstructured and you will have to infer the loop's shape from it. That is the cost of
having no tracker.

**2. The run artefacts.** `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/` — `plan.md` and `findings.md`
where PreBuild wrote them.

**3. Your own previous findings.** `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/_improver/` — what earlier
look-backs observed. **This is how you know whether something has happened before.**

**4. The current skills and agents**, and the repo, for job B.

---

## Job A — how the loop performed

For each failure you can identify, name **whose gap it was.** Be precise; the whole value is in
attributing correctly.

| Gap | Means |
|---|---|
| **Plan** | The step was underspecified, or its pass criteria were unmeasurable |
| **Implementer** | The step was clear and was implemented wrong |
| **Tester** | A defect reached the Scorer that the Tester should have caught |
| **Scorer** | Something passed that shouldn't have, or was returned without a usable instruction |
| **Brief** | **The instruction itself was wrong.** Historically the most common class on this project — eight cross-corrections against the brief in a single commit's loop. Record it plainly. |
| **Rule** | The codebase rule is wrong, missing, or contradicts another rule |

### The bar

**Any genuine defect qualifies** — a single clear failure is enough if the fix is real.

But **recurrence is the strongest signal.** Check `.runs/_improver/` before proposing: has this
class appeared before? If so, say so and say when. A pattern across two stories is worth more than
five one-offs from one, and it changes how confidently you propose.

### What is not a finding

- A one-off typo that would not recur
- Anything that traces to a decision Marcel made deliberately — report the *mechanical consequence*
  of a decision, never the decision
- "Be more careful", "add more checks", "be more thorough". If you cannot name the line to change,
  you have an observation, not a proposal

---

## Job B — citation drift

The skills cite rules, files and line numbers. Those move.

The `var(--zimm-*)` boundary **reversed direction twice in a fortnight** on this project.
`tagging.md` still describes sprint tagging that has been dead since `scripts/sprint.txt` stopped
existing. This is exactly the failure mode that made the FED handbook stale.

For every `file:line`, rule name and repo path the skills and agents cite:

- Does the file still exist?
- Does the line still say what the skill claims?
- Has the rule changed direction, not just moved?

A moved line is a citation fix. **A rule that changed direction may mean the skill's advice is now
wrong, not just its reference** — say which you think it is, and let Marcel rule.

---

## What you may change

**In scope:** `zimmerMANNPreBuild` · `zimmerMANNBuild` · `zimmerMANNPostBuild` · and the five loop
agents — `zm-planner`, `zm-orchestrator`, `zm-implementer`, `zm-tester`, `zm-scorer`.

Most failures belong in an agent brief, not a skill. A defect that reached the Scorer is a Tester
gap, and the Tester's brief is the thing to change.

**Out of bounds — never propose an edit to these:**

- `zimmerMANNReview` — that is `zimmerMANNRevImprover`'s
- `zimmerMANNSprinter`, `zimmerMANNDevOps` — different work, different evidence
- **This skill.** You do not edit your own judgement criteria.
- Anything in `zimmermann-pwa/` — Tier 1 and not ours

---

## Output

Every proposal, in this shape:

```
PROPOSAL <n> — <file>
Gap:        <plan | implementer | tester | scorer | brief | rule | citation>
Recurrence: <first seen | also seen in <ticket>, <date>>
Evidence:   <transcript turn, agent report, or file:line — quoted>
Current:    <the exact text today>
Proposed:   <the exact replacement>
Why:        <what this would have prevented, concretely>
```

**Paste-ready or it is not a proposal.**

Present them **one at a time via AskUserQuestion**, most consequential first. Apply on his explicit
go, and only the ones he approves.

---

## Always write the log

Append to `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/_improver/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md`, whether or not anything was
proposed:

```
## <date> — reviewed <tickets>
Sessions read: <n>   Agent transcripts read: <n>
Findings: <n proposed, n recorded-not-proposed>
- <gap> — <one line> — [PROPOSED / RECORDED] — <accepted / declined / pending>
Citation drift: <n checked, n stale>
Not examined: <what you could not reach>
```

**Record what you saw even when you propose nothing.** Nothing else remembers — the tracker that
would have is gone, and this log is the only way a later run can tell a second occurrence from a
first.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never edit a skill or agent without an explicit go**, one proposal at a time.
- **Never edit yourself**, `zimmerMANNReview`, `Sprinter`, `DevOps`, or anything in the repo.
- **Never propose a change you cannot cite.** Every proposal names the transcript turn, the agent
  report, or the `file:line` behind it.
- **Never propose a rewrite where an edit will do.** Small, specific, traceable.
- **Never re-litigate a decision.** If it is in `.research/DECISIONS.md` as ruled, it is settled —
  propose a consequence, not the ruling.
- **Say what you could not examine.** A session you could not find, a transcript too large to read,
  an artefact that was never written — each is itself worth knowing, and it bounds how much the
  look-back is worth.
SKILLEOF
cd ~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills && ./install.sh
echo
wc -l "$S/SKILL.md" | awk '{print "  DevImprover SKILL.md: "$1" lines"}'

content.text:
All four in. Final proposal — and one note on how they interact.

## `zimmerMANNRevImprover`

**Invocation:** `revimprove <PR#> [<PR#>…]`

### Reads

The PR itself — your review bodies, inline comments, thread resolution state, verdict transitions, and what the author did in response. Plus **the review session transcript**, found by the same ranking method DevImprover uses.

### Three jobs

**A — did each finding hold up?** Per finding: *accepted and fixed* · *disputed and you conceded* · *disputed and you held* · *silently ignored*. Those diagnose differently — a review whose findings were mostly conceded was over-reaching; one whose findings were ignored had a delivery problem, not an accuracy one.

**B — did it miss anything?** Bounded to the PR's own lifetime, since you excluded post-merge correlation: a finding CodeRabbit raised that your review didn't · a finding the author raised themselves · something a later round caught that an earlier round should have · a thread that reopened after being resolved.

**C — how was the review conducted?** From the transcript: what the agents found versus what actually got posted · what you overturned and whether you were right · what got dropped before posting · whether the ground-truth gates were genuinely run or assumed.

### What it may change

**`zimmerMANNReview` only.**

Where a failure traces to an agent's brief — `zm-tester`'s angles, `zm-scorer` in findings mode — it **reports it and names the agent, but does not edit it.** Those files belong to the build loop, and a change that helps review could quietly hurt Build. One owner per file.

### Output and log

Same proposal shape as DevImprover — file, current text, replacement, evidence, why. One at a time via AskUserQuestion, applied on your go.

Log to `.runs/_improver/rev-<date>.md` — same directory as DevImprover's, prefixed. Keeps the two improvers' histories greppable together, which matters when one reports an agent issue the other has to act on.

## One interaction worth knowing

RevImprover will surface agent-brief problems it can't fix. Those become input to DevImprover, which can. That's a deliberate handoff rather than a gap — but it means **an agent-level review problem takes two invocations to resolve.** Reasonable given the alternative is two skills editing the same files from different evidence.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `skills/zimmerMANNRevImprover/SKILL.md` | **new** |
| everything else | untouched |

Go ahead?

set -e
S=~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/skills/zimmerMANNRevImprover
mkdir -p "$S"
cat > "$S/SKILL.md" <<'SKILLEOF'
---
name: zimmerMANNRevImprover
description: Looks back over completed PR reviews and improves how Marcel reviews. Reads the PR outcome and the review session transcript to judge whether each finding held up, whether anything was missed, and how the review was actually conducted — then proposes concrete edits to zimmerMANNReview, applied only on his explicit go.
---

The look-back on review work. Not "was the PR good" — **was the review good.**

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**Input:** `$ARGUMENTS` — one or more PR numbers. `revimprove 68 70`.

**Scope: reviews Marcel gave on other people's PRs.** How he handled feedback on his own PRs is
`zimmerMANNPostBuild`'s job, and improving that is `zimmerMANNDevImprover`'s.

---

## What you read

**1. The PR outcome.**

```bash
gh api "repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/pulls/<N>/reviews"           # verdicts and their order
gh api "repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/pulls/<N>/comments?per_page=100"  # inline comments
gh api "repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/pulls/<N>/commits"           # what the author did after
```

Thread resolution needs GraphQL — the REST API does not expose `isResolved`:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='{repository(owner:"ZimmermannAU",name:"zimmermann-pwa"){
  pullRequest(number:<N>){reviewThreads(first:100){nodes{
    isResolved isOutdated comments(first:20){nodes{author{login} body path line}}}}}}}'
```

**2. The review session transcript.** Rank rather than list — a bare grep returns every passing
mention:

```bash
D=~/.claude/projects/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev-zimmermann-pwa
for f in "$D"/*.jsonl; do
  n=$(grep -oE "PR #<N>|pulls/<N>" "$f" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$n" -gt 10 ] || continue
  b=$(basename "$f" .jsonl)
  echo "$n — $b ($(find "$D/$b/subagents" -name '*.jsonl' 2>/dev/null | wc -l) agents)"
done | sort -rn
```

**3. Previous look-backs.** `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/_improver/` — both `rev-*.md` and
DevImprover's. **Check before proposing:** has this been seen before?

---

## Job A — did each finding hold up?

Classify every finding you raised:

| Outcome | Reads as |
|---|---|
| **Accepted and fixed** | The finding was right and landed |
| **Disputed, you conceded** | You were wrong, or right but at the wrong altitude |
| **Disputed, you held** | You were right and defended it — the best outcome |
| **Silently ignored** | Not an accuracy problem. A **delivery** problem. |

The ratios diagnose differently, and this is the point of the job:

- **Mostly conceded** → the review was over-reaching. Look at what class of finding kept losing —
  usually nitpicks raised at blocker weight, or house-style opinions presented as rules.
- **Mostly ignored** → the findings may have been right and the *review* failed. Wrong altitude,
  buried in noise, or no clear ask. A correct finding nobody acts on has failed.
- **Held** → find out why it survived and encode that.

---

## Job B — did it miss anything?

Bounded to the PR's own lifetime. Post-merge correlation is out of scope — a later commit touching
the same file is not proof of a missed defect.

Within the PR, four real signals:

1. **CodeRabbit raised something the review did not.** Check its findings against yours.
2. **The author raised it themselves** — in a reply, a follow-up commit, or a comment.
3. **A later round caught what an earlier round should have.** If round two found something in code
   that was unchanged since round one, round one missed it.
4. **A resolved thread reopened.**

Each is a gap in the review's coverage, and each points at an angle that was not run or not run
well.

---

## Job C — how was the review conducted?

From the transcript, not the PR. This is where process failures live.

- **What did the agents find versus what got posted?** A finding dropped before posting was either
  correctly filtered or wrongly lost. Which?
- **What did Marcel overturn — and was he right?** He adjudicates every verdict, so an overturn is a
  judgement worth checking against what actually happened.
- **Were the ground-truth gates genuinely run, or assumed?** The review's whole method rests on
  measured baselines. If they were not measured, every finding downstream inherits that.
- **Did reviewers converge or disagree?** Convergence on distinct-but-overlapping briefs is the
  confidence signal. If they all agreed because the briefs overlapped too much, that is not
  confidence, it is an echo.
- **Was anything raised that was true but unfair?** Marcel's own standard: better to drop a finding
  than post an unfair one.

---

## What you may change

**`zimmerMANNReview` only.**

Where a failure traces to an agent's brief — `zm-tester`'s angles, `zm-orchestrator`'s scope
verdict, `zm-scorer` in findings mode — **report it, name the agent and the specific brief line,
and stop.** Those files are the build loop's, and a change that helps review could quietly hurt
Build. `zimmerMANNDevImprover` or Marcel makes that edit.

Say plainly in the report that the item needs a second pass to resolve. Do not work around it.

**Never edit:** the `zm-*` agents · `zimmerMANNPreBuild`, `Build`, `PostBuild`, `Sprinter`,
`DevOps` · **this skill** · anything in `zimmermann-pwa/`.

---

## Output

```
PROPOSAL <n> — skills/zimmerMANNReview/SKILL.md
Job:        <A finding-quality | B coverage-gap | C process>
Recurrence: <first seen | also seen in PR #<n>, <date>>
Evidence:   <PR thread, transcript turn, or agent report — quoted>
Current:    <the exact text today>
Proposed:   <the exact replacement>
Why:        <what this would have changed about that review, concretely>
```

Agent-brief findings use the same shape but end `Owner: zm-tester — for DevImprover or you`, with
no `Proposed` block.

**Paste-ready or it is not a proposal.** One at a time via AskUserQuestion, most consequential
first. Applied on his explicit go.

---

## Always write the log

Append to `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/_improver/rev-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md`, proposals or not:

```
## <date> — reviewed PR #<n>, #<n>
Findings raised: <n>  | fixed <n> · conceded <n> · held <n> · ignored <n>
Coverage gaps: <n>   (CodeRabbit <n>, author-raised <n>, late-round <n>, reopened <n>)
Process notes: <n>
Proposals: <n>  | accepted <n> · declined <n> · pending <n>
Handed to DevImprover: <agent-brief items, or none>
Not examined: <what you could not reach>
```

**Record what you saw even when you propose nothing.** Nothing else remembers — this log is how a
later run knows a second occurrence from a first.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never edit anything without an explicit go**, one proposal at a time.
- **Never edit an agent brief.** Report it and hand it over.
- **Never propose a change you cannot cite** to a PR thread, a transcript turn, or a `file:line`.
- **Never judge the PR.** You are judging the review of it. A PR that shipped fine after a bad
  review is still a bad review, and a rejected PR after a good one is still a good review.
- **Never re-litigate a ruling** in `.research/DECISIONS.md`.
- **Say what you could not examine** — a transcript you could not find, threads the API would not
  return, a review conducted before the skill existed.

cd ~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills && ./install.sh
echo
wc -l "$S/SKILL.md" | awk '{print "  RevImprover SKILL.md: "$1" lines"}'

set -e
cat > ~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/README.md <<'EOF'
# zimmerMANN-skills

Marcel Navarro's personal FED Lead workflow skills for the Zimmermann PWA Kit.

These are **mine**, not the team's. The repo's own skills (`zimmermann-pwa/.claude/skills/`) are
authored by Tim and Hardi and encode how *the codebase* works. These encode how *I* work. They
**call** the repo's skills — they never duplicate or bypass them.

Built 2026-08-30 from a full read of 459 sessions and 309 agent transcripts. The evidence is in
`.research/FINDINGS.md`; every design ruling is in `.research/DECISIONS.md`. **Read DECISIONS.md
before changing anything, and do not re-litigate what it records.**

---

## The skills

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| **`zimmerMANNPreBuild`** | Starting any story. Gathers Jira, Confluence, the handbook, the codebase and Figma; gates on every gap; writes the plan. |
| **`zimmerMANNBuild`** | Executing an approved plan. Runs the loop per step, commits each, and handles rework after a PR is open. |
| **`zimmerMANNPostBuild`** | After a build. Audits against the plan and findings, sweeps the whole feature, writes the PR, owns the review conversation. |
| **`zimmerMANNReview`** | Reviewing someone else's PR. Ground truth, fan-out audit, verified findings — I adjudicate. |
| **`zimmerMANNDevOps`** | Deploys, promotions, tags, release cuts, rollback. Verifies live state before anything moves. |
| **`zimmerMANNSprinter`** | Ceremonies. `refine` · `plan` · `standup` · `retro` · `prep` for any meeting. |
| **`zimmerMANNDevImprover`** | Looking back over build work. Diagnoses where the loop failed and proposes edits. |
| **`zimmerMANNRevImprover`** | Looking back over reviews. Did the findings hold up, did anything get missed. |

## The chain

```
  PreBuild ──▶ .runs/<TICKET>/plan.md + findings.md
     │              (presents, then STOPS — never invokes Build)
     ▼
  Build    ──▶ loop per step: implement → test → scope → score → rework (max 3)
     │         ⏸  visual checkpoint — I look at the page
     │         commits each passing step
     └──────▶ .runs/<TICKET>/handoff.md
     ▼
  PostBuild ─▶ audits plan + findings · whole-feature sweep · writes the PR
     │         ⏸  presents, then STOPS
     │         on my go: pushes, opens PR
     │
     └─ review findings ──▶ Build `rework` ──▶ back to PostBuild
                                              ⏸  replies posted on my go

  Review     stands alone — someone else's PR
  DevOps     stands alone — ⏸ every action on my go
  Sprinter   stands alone — ⏸ Jira writes on my go

  DevImprover  ──▶ may edit PreBuild · Build · PostBuild · the zm-* agents
  RevImprover  ──▶ may edit Review only; hands agent issues to DevImprover
                   both log to .runs/_improver/
```

**⏸ marks a human gate.** Nothing outward-facing happens without me.

---

## Rules these skills hold to

1. **Never write to the repo's Claude Code config.** `zimmermann-pwa/.claude/**`, `AGENTS.md`,
   `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, `.docs/memory/**` and `.docs/prd/**` are Tier 1 Governance.
   Feature code, commits and PRs are in scope. Config is not.
2. **Human-in-the-lead.** No hooks, no triggers. Nothing fires unless I invoke it.
3. **Reuse over reimplementation.** `/session-start`, `/feature-spec`, `/scope-check`,
   `/audit-tier`, `/code-quality`, `/pr-checklist`, `/generate-changelog`,
   `/upstream-sync-review`, `/zimmermann-pwa:code-review` already exist. Call them.
4. **Stop before anything outward-facing.** Push, PR-open, posted comments and Jira writes wait
   for me.
5. **Scale to the work.** A two-point story does not get the full loop. No overthinking.
6. **Local-only docs are never citable** in a PR, commit or code comment. Cite `AGENTS.md` or
   `.claude/rules/*` instead.
7. **Say what you could not verify.** Silence reads as "nothing wrong" when it may mean
   "didn't look there".

## The agents

| Agent | Model | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `zm-planner` | opus | PreBuild |
| `zm-implementer` | sonnet | Build |
| `zm-tester` | sonnet | Build · PostBuild · Review |
| `zm-orchestrator` | sonnet | Build · PostBuild · Review |
| `zm-scorer` | sonnet | Build (six axes) · Review (findings mode) |

## Layout

```
skills/<name>/SKILL.md    symlinked into ~/.claude/skills/
agents/<name>.md          symlinked into ~/.claude/agents/
.runs/<TICKET>/           plan.md · findings.md · handoff.md   (gitignored)
.runs/_improver/          look-back logs, both improvers        (gitignored)
.research/                FINDINGS.md · DECISIONS.md · DEVOPS-STATE.md
```

## Install

```bash
./install.sh
```

Creates the symlinks that make the skills and agents discoverable. Re-run after adding either.

cd ~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills && ./install.sh >/dev/null && echo "  README rewritten as the map"

Path flags were regex artefacts — everything resolves. Atlassian MCP is enabled, so Sprinter works. Here's what's actually left.

## Real gaps, ranked

**1. There's no git in `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/`.** No history, no diffs, no recovery. This has already cost us once — I overwrote the six v1 agents and had to reconstruct them from session context because nothing had a copy. The `.gitignore` exists and does nothing without a repo. One command fixes it, and it's the difference between a bad edit being an `undo` and being a rewrite.

**2. PostBuild persists nothing.** We closed Build → PostBuild with `handoff.md`, but PostBuild's audit and sweep results go nowhere. Two consequences: the reverse leg — Build `rework` → PostBuild — has exactly the cross-session gap we just fixed on the forward leg, and DevImprover has no record of what PostBuild found, only what Build did.

**3. `zimmerMANNReview` states no model intent.** Every other skill names one. Trivial, but it's the kind of inconsistency that reads as an oversight later.

**4. The improvers have nothing to improve from.** `DevImprover` wants sessions where the skills were used; `RevImprover` wants reviews conducted with `zimmerMANNReview`. Neither exists. Pointed at your history today they'd re-derive the research we already did. This resolves itself the moment you run a real story — it's just worth knowing they're inert until then.

**5. Nothing has met a real ticket.** The one that matters. Every design ruling is reasoned from 459 sessions of evidence, and none of it has been exercised. The first run will surface things this audit structurally cannot — a mode that reads well and executes badly, a preflight that's too slow to tolerate, a gate that fires when it shouldn't.

## Confirmed not gaps

Every file path resolves · every agent reference resolves · all eight skills have Hard rules · all nine reused repo skills exist · `.runs/` structure intact · CodeRabbit correctly split three ways.

## What I'd do

**1 and 3 now** — git init plus a one-line model statement, five minutes, and #1 protects everything else we do.

**2 is a real decision** — it means editing PostBuild again, and you've twice chosen transcript-reading over adding artefact writes. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.

**4 and 5 only resolve by using it.** The most useful next move isn't more building — it's running `zimmerMANNPreBuild` against a live ticket and seeing what breaks.

Want me to do 1 and 3?

Here's the board. You have two active: **SFCC-102** (Tech design, Contentful slide-out) and **SFCC-132** (Blocked). Neither is ideal for a first run — one isn't build-ready, the other can't start.

**My pick: SFCC-841 "Checkout Footer – PWA Kit Component"** — To Do, unassigned, Squad-A, Medium. Small, and crucially **precedented**: the Global Footer already shipped in PR #59, which is the exemplar every skill measures against. You'd need to assign it to yourself.

## Optimal first-run order

The chain order isn't the test order. Escalate by risk — read-only before write, cheap before expensive.

**Phase 0 — smoke tests, zero risk**

```
/zimmerMANNDevOps status
```
Pure read. Confirms `gh`, the repo and the environment ladder all resolve. If the plumbing is broken you find out in 30 seconds rather than mid-build. Expect it to be slow — you chose full pipeline health on every invocation.

```
/zimmerMANNSprinter refine SFCC-841
```
Also pure read. Exercises Jira, Confluence and Figma, and tells you whether the ticket is even sizeable. If refinement says it's blocked on design, stop — you've tested the gate and saved a build.

**Phase 1 — the gate**

```
/zimmerMANNPreBuild SFCC-841
```
Still writes nothing outside `.runs/`. Produces `plan.md` and `findings.md`, presents, **stops**. This is where I'd expect the first real friction — five parallel source checks, and the Figma section now demands a node URL per variant *and* state.

**Phase 2 — the build.** Create the branch yourself first; PreBuild won't, and the `PreToolUse` hook blocks all edits on `develop`.

```
/zimmerMANNBuild SFCC-841
```
The loop. **Have the dev server running** — the visual checkpoint halts everything until you've looked.

**Phase 3 — the PR**

```
/zimmerMANNPostBuild SFCC-841
```
Audit, sweep, PR body, writes `postbuild.md`, stops before push.

**Phase 4 — the point of the exercise**

```
/zimmerMANNDevImprover SFCC-841
```
This is what turns a test into learning. It reads all four artefacts and the transcript and tells you where the chain actually failed.

`zimmerMANNReview` tests independently — point it at an open PR you haven't reviewed. It's read-only until you approve posting.

## Three things I'd expect to bite

**Build's preflight runs on every step**, and you chose full pipeline health over speed. On a five-step story that's a lot of repeated API calls. Worth seeing whether it's tolerable or wants scoping.

**The Storybook gate is under-specified** — there's no `test-storybook` script, and `test:story` turns out to be BrowserStack. The skill says "build it, serve it on a verified-free port"; nailing the actual command is a first-run job.

**The visual checkpoint is a hard stop.** If you step away mid-build, the loop waits. Correct behaviour, but it means the loop isn't unattended.

Want me to pull SFCC-841 in full so we can see whether it's genuinely a good candidate before you commit to it?

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNPreBuild

The gate before code. Nothing gets built until every source has been checked and every gap has
been named.

**Intended model: Opus 5 at maximum effort.** A skill cannot pin the session model — set it
yourself before invoking. The plan synthesis step delegates to the `zm-planner` agent, which is
pinned to Opus regardless of the session model, so the expensive judgement runs on Opus either
way.

**Input:** `SFCC-91` — a Jira key (e.g. `SFCC-194`), optionally followed by a depth.
If no key is given, ask for one before doing anything else.

## Depth

Depth is a parameter, not an adverb. Pick one and say which you are using:

| Depth | Jira + Confluence | Codebase | Figma |
|---|---|---|---|
| `quick` | the ticket and its direct links | branch state, file tiers | the named node only |
| `standard` *(default)* | ticket, links, comments; targeted Confluence search | tiers, blast radius, nearest existing pattern | node, variants, states |
| `exhaustive` | full link graph, all comments, related epics, all matching Confluence | above, plus every consumer of every touched file and the exemplar PR diffs | node, all variants, all states, all viewports, token mapping |

Never substitute a stronger adverb for a depth. "In-depth full-on exhaustive" is not a level;
`exhaustive` is.

---

## Phase 0 — position

Call `/session-start`. It confirms the branch, reads the tracking docs, runs health checks and
states current position.

Then confirm one thing it does not: **you cannot be on `develop` or `main`.** A `PreToolUse` hook
blocks every Write and Edit on those branches, so a plan handed to the builder from `develop` is
dead on arrival. If the branch is wrong, say so and stop — do not create a branch unasked.

---

## Phase 1 — gather

Run these **in parallel**. Each one ends in its own findings block. Never let a clean source hide
a broken one — report all five, even when four are fine.

### Jira — `mcp__mcp-atlassian__jira_get_issue`

Pull the story and read all of it: description, requirements, acceptance criteria, linked design,
attachments, linked work items, and the full comment thread. Comments routinely carry the
decision that contradicts the description.

Flag: missing or untestable ACs · requirements that contradict each other or the comments ·
no linked design · attachments referenced in prose but not attached · linked work items that are
still open and block this one · a decision made in comments that never made it into the description.

### Confluence — `confluence_search`, `confluence_get_page`

Search for anything bearing on this story: TSDs, integration docs, data dictionaries, decisions.

Flag: no TSD where the work clearly needs one · a TSD that contradicts the ticket · documentation
describing an approach the codebase does not implement · a page last updated before a decision
that supersedes it.

### FED handbook — `~/Dev/fed-handbook.md`

The build approach: tokens, components, CSS structure, overriding, accessibility, tests, stories.
Part I is the machine, Part II the procedure, Part III the role.

Flag: handbook guidance that contradicts what the codebase now does · a claim whose cited
`file:line` no longer resolves · anything the story needs that the handbook does not cover.

The handbook is a derived account, not the source. **Where it disagrees with
`.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md`, that file wins** — and say so, because it means the handbook
is stale.

### Codebase

Branch state, and the shape of what is about to be touched.

- Confirm `develop` is current with `origin/develop`.
- For every likely-touched file: tier and owner, from `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md` and
  `protectedFiles.md`. **Never from `.claude/registry/*.md`** — its Tier column is a derived
  heuristic and is wrong in places.
- Call `/audit-tier <path>` for anything you are unsure about. It also returns import blast radius.
- Find the nearest existing pattern. This codebase has strong precedent; matching it is cheaper
  and more reviewable than inventing.
- Read the exemplar PRs when the story touches their surface: **PR #59** (component + CSS layer,
  focused vs shared recipes) and **PR #56** (the token layer).

Flag: any Tier 1 file in the likely set · high blast radius (a shared file with many consumers) ·
work that crosses squad territory · an existing pattern the story would contradict.

### Figma

- Design System 2026 — `https://www.figma.com/design/wPiWmZZOVKnrENUWk2XWWm/Zimmermann_Design_System_2026`
- Zimmermann_Designs — `https://www.figma.com/design/QQ427wHWEUjsjP7H8v48Rs/Zimmermann_Designs`

**Ask for one node URL per variant and per state**, not one per component. If the file-level
links are not enough to resolve the specific component, stop and ask Marcel. Do not guess at
which node the story means, and do not build from a neighbouring node that looks close.

Check:

- **Completeness** — every variant and every state: hover, focus, active, disabled, loading,
  error, empty, success.
- **Currency** — is this design archived or superseded? Triage archived against current before
  anyone builds to it. An archived node that still renders is a trap.
- **Tokenisation** — does every value map to an existing `--zimm-*` token, or is a new token
  being introduced? A new token is Tier 1 and needs the designer.
- **Responsiveness** — frames exist at 402 / 1023 / 1440; breakpoint tokens are 768 / 860 / 1024.
  **The 768–1022 band is unframed**, so anything in it is an inference, not a design.

Two measurement traps that have produced false defects here. Flag a comparison that hits either:

- **Node type decides comparability.** Figma TEXT nodes report a cap-height box, which is not
  comparable to a CSS line box — never file a mismatch from one. FRAMES and INSTANCES report a
  real box and are directly comparable.
- **The two Figma files must never be cross-compared.** The Design System file and the Designs
  file are different sources; a delta between them is not a defect.

**No design is a blocker, not licence to invent.** If the ACs name something Figma does not have,
that is a finding for Marcel — or an explicit **provisional**, labelled as such and carried into
the plan as an assumption. Never fill the gap silently.

Flag: missing variants or states · a design that is archived or superseded · values with no token
· the unframed tablet band left to inference · a design that contradicts an established component
· no design at all where the story implies one.

---

## Phase 2 — reuse

These already exist. Call them; do not reimplement them.

1. `/feature-spec` — turns the gathered picture into a scoped implementation plan and emits a
   ready-to-paste scoped prompt.
2. `/scope-check` — run it **on that prompt**. It verdicts SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED and rewrites
   risky prompts. This is the highest-leverage gate available; do not skip it.
3. `/audit-tier <path>` — per file, wherever scope-check flags something specific.

Two known traps when calling these:

- `/code-quality` defaults to diffing against **`main`**; `/pr-checklist` diffs against
  **`develop`**. On a feature branch these give different file sets. Always pass explicit scope.
- `/pr-checklist` already calls `/code-quality` internally. Calling both doubles the audit.

None of these skills emits machine-readable output — they all return prose for a human. If you
need to branch on a result, restate the verdict yourself rather than parsing theirs.

---

## Phase 3 — the gate

This is the part that earns the skill. Produce one table, every source, every gap:

| # | Source | Finding | Severity | What unblocks it |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Severity is one of:

- 🔴 **BLOCKED** — cannot plan around it. A missing AC, an absent design, a Tier 1 file with no
  owner approval, a `scope-check` BLOCKED verdict. **Stop here.** Report and wait for Marcel.
- 🟡 **CLARIFY** — plannable, but the plan carries a stated assumption. Name the assumption
  explicitly in the plan so it is visible if it turns out wrong.
- 🔵 **NOTE** — worth knowing, does not affect the plan.

**Do not fill a gap with an assumption and carry on silently.** A missing acceptance criterion is
a finding, not something to infer. The whole point of the gate is that it stops.

---

## Phase 4 — plan

Delegate to the `zm-planner` agent (Opus). Give it everything gathered — all five findings blocks,
the `/feature-spec` output, and the `/scope-check` verdict.

It returns: goal statement · scale call (multi-commit or multi-branch, with reasoning) · file
manifest with tiers and owners · steps with concrete pass criteria · per-step loop configuration ·
open questions.

Write the result to `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/plan.md`, and write the Phase 3 gate
table to `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/findings.md`.

Create the run directory if it does not exist. **Never write run state into the repo.**

---

## Phase 5 — handoff

Present to Marcel, in **"ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead"** register — not dumbed down, but without
jargon that gets in the way. Lead with the consequence, then the mechanism, then the fix.

1. The gate table — blockers first.
2. The plan summary — scale call, step count, file count with tier breakdown.
3. Every stated assumption, gathered in one place.
4. The paths to `plan.md` and `findings.md`.

Then say plainly whether this is ready for `zimmerMANNBuild`, or what is blocking it.

**Put decisions to him one at a time, using AskUserQuestion.** Do not present a wall of choices
and do not bundle unrelated calls into one question.

**This skill stops here. It never invokes `zimmerMANNBuild`** — Marcel does, once he has read the
gate. Discover → report → wait for approval → and execution is a separate, deliberate act.

**Do not hand off with an unresolved 🔴.** Handing a blocked plan to the builder is how a
build burns an afternoon on the wrong thing.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never modify anything.** This skill reads, checks and plans. The only files it writes are
  under `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/`. No repo file is touched — not one.
- **Never write to the repo's config** — `zimmermann-pwa/.claude/**`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
  `CODEOWNERS`, `.docs/memory/**`, `.docs/prd/**`. All Tier 1 Governance.
- **Never infer squad ownership** from `squadA.md` / `squadB.md`. They contradict each other on
  PDP/PLP and are both drafts. Read `CODEOWNERS`.
- **Never present a gap as resolved because it seems minor.** Report it and let Marcel decide.
- **Say what you did not check.** A source you skipped is itself a finding.
- **Provenance, not proximity.** A document living in the codebase is a downstream artifact, not
  a source. If you cannot locate the original source for a claim, flag it **provenance unknown**
  and ask. Never fabricate a source, and never fall back to citing a codebase path as one.
- **Local-only docs are never citable.** `~/Dev/fed-handbook.md` and its predecessors are
  Marcel's personal files. **They must never appear in a PR, a commit message, or a code
  comment.** Where the same rule exists in `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/*`, cite the repo file
  instead — that is the citable source.
- **Scale to the work.** A two-point story does not get the full treatment. At `quick` depth,
  drop the exemplar-PR read and the blast-radius sweep, and keep the gate. Nothing too crazy,
  no overthinking.

Run the mandatory session start ritual defined in [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md). Do this before writing any code.

## Steps (in order — do not skip any)

1. **Confirm branch** — run `git branch --show-current`. If the output is `develop` or `main`, stop immediately — no edits permitted (see [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) Hard Rule 1). If it matches `release/*` or `hotfix/*`, read [.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md](../../../.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md) in full before proceeding — the supervised-edit and back-merge rules there apply on top of the Hard Rules.

2. **Read tracking docs** — read these in parallel:
   - [.docs/memory/projectState.md](../../../.docs/memory/projectState.md) — current phase, integration statuses (mock/live/not started), what's done and pending
   - [.docs/memory/sprintScope.md](../../../.docs/memory/sprintScope.md) — what exists this sprint, what is deferred. **Read before scoping any new work.**
   - [.docs/memory/feedback.md](../../../.docs/memory/feedback.md) — patterns to avoid or repeat
   - [.docs/memory/upstreamBaseline.md](../../../.docs/memory/upstreamBaseline.md) — current `@salesforce/retail-react-app` version and review state
   - [../session-notes.md](../session-notes.md) — lightweight, **gitignored, per-developer** carryover notes from your last local session (a Claude-writable staging area — see "Living Memory" below for how this differs from `.docs/memory/`). If it has pending items, surface them in step 4's "blockers or outstanding issues" and clear/promote each once resolved. It won't exist for a fresh clone or a teammate who hasn't used it — that's expected, skip silently.

3. **Health checks** — run when the helper exists:
   - `bash scripts/healthCheckAll.sh` — If the script does not exist yet, state that clearly and skip.

4. **State current position** — in plain language, say exactly:
   - Current branch
   - Current sprint / phase (from `projectState.md`)
   - The last completed task and the next task
   - Any blockers or outstanding issues

   Format: "Resuming from: [last completed task]. Next: [next task]. [Any blockers or health issues]."

5. **Confirm readiness** — ask if the user wants to proceed with the stated next task or redirect to something else.

Do not write any code until this ritual is complete and the user has confirmed direction.

---

## Living Memory — what belongs where

`.docs/memory/` is the project's persistent memory. Keep it current — update the relevant file whenever a session produces new information that belongs there.

**`.claude/session-notes.md` is different: a lightweight, Claude-writable, gitignored, per-developer staging area** (same pattern as `userProfile.md` below, but for tasks rather than profile info) for short-lived carryover items (e.g. "still need to do X next session") that haven't been promoted to `.docs/memory/` yet. It's **not** shared via git — each developer's notes stay local, so they never conflict or overwrite a teammate's. Unlike the files below, Claude may write to it directly. Use it for quick pending-item tracking; move anything durable and team-relevant into the right `.docs/memory/` file once it's confirmed, and clear the note.

| File | What belongs there | When to update |
|---|---|---|
| `architecture.md` | Stack decisions, overrides pattern, key paths, structural choices | A new integration is added, a structural decision is made, or a key path changes |
| `projectState.md` | Phase, integration statuses (mock/live/not started), what's done and pending, unresolved dependencies | Any integration goes live, a phase changes, a feature is completed, or a dependency is resolved |
| `feedback.md` | What worked, what failed, patterns to avoid or repeat | After discovering a gotcha, a failed approach, or a validated pattern |
| `references.md` | Service URLs, API keys, credentials, logins, dashboards | A new credential or service URL is introduced (system roles live in `architecture.md`) |
| `userProfile.md` | User's role, expertise, working style, preferences | User shares a preference or working-style detail that should persist |

**Rules:**
- Never leave a file with only its placeholder comment — populate it the moment you learn something that belongs there.
- **No duplication.** Every fact has exactly one home. Before writing something, check whether it already lives in another doc — if it does, reference that doc instead of copying. Applies across all `.md` files: `AGENTS.md`, memory files, and PRDs.
- **Conciseness.** Keep all `.md` instructions concise.
